description: Engines began replacing draught animals. John Froelich's petrol tractor worked Iowa's 1892 threshing season; Benjamin Holt tested a tracked steam tractor on Californian peat in 1904. Mass-produced Fordsons followed from 1917, and combines reaped and threshed in one pass. Machinery helped shrink US farm work from over a third of workers in 1900 to under 2 percent by 2000.

claims: Froelich petrol tractor, Iowa, 1892 threshing season
Holt horse-drawn combine 1886 (combine lineage)
Holt tracked steam tractor first tested at Stockton, 1904, on peat soils
Fordson mass production from 1917
US farm labour share about 41 percent in 1900 to 1.9 percent in 2000; machinery a driver
mechanisation contributed to long-term decline of US farm employment

uncertainty: Over 100 crawler-tread patents preceded Holt's, though his was the first practical field design; the 1900 US farm labour share is estimated between about 36 and 41 percent. The labour figures are for the United States only; timing and extent of mechanisation differed widely by region, farm size and access to capital.

description: Drip irrigation releases water slowly at the roots through plastic emitters, wasting less than flooding or sprinklers. Perforated-pipe trials predate it, but Israeli engineer Simcha Blass found that long, narrow passages inside an emitter slowed flow without the clogging of tiny holes. Tested at Kibbutz Hatzerim in the Negev, the design was commercialised by Netafim, founded in 1965.

claims: Blass used long passages and friction inside a plastic emitter instead of tiny holes that clogged
first trials at Kibbutz Hatzerim, Negev
Netafim founded 1965; first sales 1967
drip irrigation conserves agricultural water; Blass and Hatzerim origin

uncertainty: Accounts date Blass's first prototypes to 1959 or 1960 and the kibbutz partnership to 1964 or 1965; earlier subsurface and perforated-pipe watering experiments existed in several countries.

factCheck.notes: Corroborated: Blass emitter principle, Hatzerim, Netafim 1965. Not corroborated by search: the existence of earlier perforated-pipe trials and the comparative water saving against flooding or sprinklers (general knowledge, stated cautiously).

description: Precision agriculture treats a field as a patchwork rather than a uniform unit. In the early 1990s, yield monitors on combines logged grain flow against satellite positions, and the maps showed yields varying within fields. Variable-rate machines, adopted from the late 1990s, adjusted seed and fertiliser by location. Uptake was uneven: early returns were inconsistent and data standards lagged.

claims: yield monitor commercially available 1992
yield monitors logged against GPS showed within-field variation; Australia from 1993
variable-rate technology among early adopters in the late 1990s
civil GPS available early 1990s; missing standards slowed uptake

uncertainty: Start dates vary by source and country: variable-rate fertiliser research from 1983, yield monitors 1992-1993, auto-steering from 1996; most sources are trade or industry histories.

description: Crop genomics reads and edits the DNA of food plants to guide breeding. The rice genome, published in 2005 by a project begun in 1997, mapped about 37,500 genes and became a reference for related cereals. Breeders pair such maps with editing tools like CRISPR, which alters chosen sites without leaving foreign DNA; rules for it vary by country.

claims: rice genome published 2005; project established 1997; about 37,544 genes; reference for related cereals
genomics combined with genome editing for breeding goals; unclear legal status of edited crops
editing changes specific sites without leaving foreign DNA
regulatory treatment of edited crops differs between countries

uncertainty: Rice sequence completion is dated 2004 in one review and published 2005; how much yield gain genome editing will deliver at field scale remains an open research question.

description: Climate engineering means deliberate, large-scale intervention in the climate system. A 2009 Royal Society report split proposals into two families: removing carbon dioxide from the air, and reflecting some sunlight back to space. It judged removal preferable; reflection could cool quickly but would not lower carbon dioxide, and no method had been shown affordable with acceptable environmental effects.

claims: two families: carbon dioxide removal and solar radiation management
CDR preferable to SRM
SRM cools rapidly but does not affect CO2
no method yet shown affordable with acceptable impacts
geoengineering as deliberate large-scale intervention in the climate system

uncertainty: Feasibility, side effects and governance of both families, especially sunlight reflection, remain scientifically and politically contested; assessments after 2009 were not checked here.

description: Scientific plant breeding applied Mendel's laws to crops. In 1905 Cambridge's Rowland Biffen showed that wheat's yellow-rust resistance was inherited in Mendelian fashion. In 1908 George Shull, and independently Edward East, described hybrid vigour in crosses of inbred maize. Hybrid seed, sold from 1926 and rebought yearly, covered 6 percent of Iowa's corn in 1935 and nearly all by 1942.

claims: Biffen 1905: rust susceptibility in wheat a Mendelian character
Biffen bred resistant Little Joss (1910) using this knowledge
Shull 1908 hybrid vigour from crossing pure lines; East independently
Iowa hybrid share 6 percent 1935 to about 99 percent 1942
hybrid seed bought each year
Hi-Bred Corn Co. founded 1926 to produce hybrid seed corn

uncertainty: One local history dates Biffen's demonstration to 1906; other seed firms may have offered hybrid seed in the early 1920s, so 1926 marks a company founding rather than the first sale. Hybrid uptake was fastest in the US Corn Belt and slower elsewhere.
